HEADLINE: Business puts 'sacred cows' on table
INTRO: Business leaders said the tax debate had to consider the "sacred cows" including superannuation, negative gearing and land tax, in addition to the GST.
TEXT:
Business leaders said the tax debate had to consider the "sacred cows" including superannuation, negative gearing and land tax, in addition to the GST.

Financial Services Council chief executive Sally Loane said superannuation, which costs $32 billion a year and provides generous tax breaks to higher income earners, had to be part of the debate.

"Issues, which are being fiercely contested in the public arena right now such as the family home, tax treatment of superannuation, the pension assets and income tests, personal and company tax rates, the GST and capital gains - all should be considered in the review," Ms Loane said.

Company director and AMP chairman Simon McKeon said all the "sacred cows", including whether we had the right age pension policy, had to be part of the discussion, in a way they hadn't been in the past.

"At the end of the day, if we're going to have a big review we need to have it about everything," he said. "I am worried that we have got stymied, that we have created some sacred cows for not necessarily a good reason," he said.

Clayton Utz partner Mark Friezer said negative gearing, dividend imputation and land tax should be considered.

"It's time to take a hard look at negative gearing," said Mr Friezer, who called it an extension of welfare to the wealthy through "overly generous tax subsidies". Instead, interest deductions should be quarantined against passive income and excess carried forward.

He also questioned the 50 per cent discount on capital gains tax for long-held assets, and said that dividend imputations was "almost a weapon of mass destruction for super funds".

Mr Friezer admitted that some of the ideas would hurt the income tax returns of many in the short term, including his own.

ACOSS chief executive Cassandra Goldie agreed that land tax could be part of the solution. "Land doesn't move and we can see over the last decade or so the way in which there have been significant rises in the value of property [that have not been] reflected in the tax take on land."

The tax discussion paper, released on Monday, singles out stamp duty and company tax as the least efficient taxes and the GST as one of the more efficient.

Business Council of Australia president Catherine Livingstone said the government should use reform process to "map out a plan for significantly reducing the company tax rate", and said the prime minister's position that change will only be pursued if the states agreed, "puts a very high hurdle" on reform.

Clayton Utz's Mr Friezer said that it was not just about increasing the rate. "GST itself has a structural problem - collections have been steadily falling as consumption has trended towards untaxed education, health and rent."

The 2010 Henry review found 10 per cent of revenue was raised by 115 taxes, roughly half of them levied by states.

"The inconsistent duty regimes in each state - in particular, duty on sale of business and inconsistent corporate reconstruction relief - distorts market behaviours and inhibits sensible and efficient transactions," said company director and chairman of ShineWing, James MacKenzie.

Mr MacKenzie said payroll tax made Australia "less competitive compared with foreign countries when global companies make decisions on where to locate their mobile workforce" and called for the replacement of stamp duty on the family home with a broader-based land tax.

He said state tax reform was inextricably tied to the GST. "It is impossible to obtain state taxation reform without either increasing the GST rate or the GST base," he said.

He would also like to see employee share scheme rules that better match commercial reality, winding back the 2009 changes that taxed shares on vesting, to "allow Australian business to attract and retain the key talent required to reverse the brain drain".

Mr McKeon urged a focus on simpler system. "We have an incredibly complicated tax system," he said.

"I know enough people who do know a lot about tax who actually say that we have a system that has grown over decades and it's had hundreds of bandaids applied," Mr1 McKeon said.

"You've got to be an expert and even the experts would say we have by global standards, a very complex tax system."

HEADLINE: Changes to the mix offer growth-friendly reform, but GST is key
INTRO: Tony Abbott is trying to put the onus on the people and the premiers.
TEXT:
Tony Abbott is trying to put the onus on the people and the premiers.

The government, the discussion paper says, won't change the GST without broad public support and unanimous state approval.

Yet, the most powerful tax reform under consideration - a cut in personal and corporate income tax rates - is impossible without a significant shift in the revenue burden to either the GST or other, even more controversial, taxes such as payroll tax, or a completely new tax on business turnover or an expanded land tax.

Increasing the GST rate appears to be the government's reform of choice, probably because it can be justified most easily by reference to the much higher rates elsewhere.

Australia's GST rate is about half that of those imposed by other rich economies.

However, if the government can expand the GST tax base it should. As the discussion paper points out, the exemptions in the GST tax base are an inefficient way to help lower-income earners, not least because high-income earners spend more on GST-exempt goods and services than do low-income earners.

It would be smarter to broaden the GST base and generously compensate low-income households for the increase in their living costs.

Australia's GST covers only about 47 per cent of the potential consumption tax base. New Zealand's covers about 96 per cent and yet, on the standard measure used by economists, its income distribution is only about as unequal as ours.

Surely we can manage that.

A shift in the tax burden from corporate and other income tax to GST has been identified by economists as one of the more effective ways to boost economic activity over the next decade or so.

That's mainly because of the powerful net long-term benefits, with lower personal and company tax rates increasing investment and, therefore, labour productivity (with most of the benefit going to workers in the longer term) and with the offsetting increase in GST having relatively little adverse impact on economic activity.

However, changing the tax mix also has an important short-term benefit.

Many economic reforms involve substantial up-front adjustment costs, with the benefits coming later as labour and capital are re-employed in more productive activities.

But analysis by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development of 30 years of reform in its member states has found that cuts in the share of corporate and personal income taxes quickly reduce unemployment, particularly for young people.

The growth-friendly way to offset the loss of revenue, the OECD has found, is to shift the burden towards taxes on less mobile and responsive bases, such as consumption.

HEADLINE: Newman's western plane
INTRO: Climate sceptic and Tony Abbott's top business adviser Maurice Newman might not hug trees, but he does love animals - even if he's not too concerned about the air they breathe. In his capacity as chairman of the Taronga Foundation, Newman flew to Dubbo on Monday for a community event at Taronga's Western Plains outpost - the single-biggest tourist attraction in Dubbo since it lost the 1988 Olympics to Seoul (a visiting Juan Antonio Samaranch landed a nasty case of gastro after a slice of the CWA's frozen carrot cake).
TEXT:
Climate sceptic and Tony Abbott's top business adviser Maurice Newman might not hug trees, but he does love animals - even if he's not too concerned about the air they breathe. In his capacity as chairman of the Taronga Foundation, Newman flew to Dubbo on Monday for a community event at Taronga's Western Plains outpost - the single-biggest tourist attraction in Dubbo since it lost the 1988 Olympics to Seoul (a visiting Juan Antonio Samaranch landed a nasty case of gastro after a slice of the CWA's frozen carrot cake).

Newman took the same QantasLink turbo prop as Alan Joyce - funny, given Newman is a director of Jetstar's direct rival Tiger Air, owned by Qantas's direct rival Virgin Australia. Qantas is a supporter of the zoo, which the airline's head office has ceased to resemble since I left the building and also in case you were worried about Joyce's choice of holiday destination.

HEADLINE: Babcock boys cream it with Scone sale
INTRO: It was back in 2005 when a consortium of Babcock & Brown high-flyers, including chieftains Phil Green and Lance Rosenberg, paid $23 million for Glenrock Station - a 30,000-hectare property outside Scone in the Upper Hunter, alongside the Packer family's Ellerston estate. It must seem like a lifetime ago.
TEXT:
It was back in 2005 when a consortium of Babcock & Brown high-flyers, including chieftains Phil Green and Lance Rosenberg, paid $23 million for Glenrock Station - a 30,000-hectare property outside Scone in the Upper Hunter, alongside the Packer family's Ellerston estate. It must seem like a lifetime ago.

A decade later, the financiers have offloaded the property, exchanging on Friday with a Chinese buyer for the princely sum of $45 million.

We're sure the Foreign Investment Review Board will be taking a look at that one.

According to ASIC filings, Green owns 51 per cent of the property's holding company, Glenrock Station Pty Ltd, and its directors include Claymore Capital's Anton Rosenberg (whose wife Sharron is also a shareholder) and former Babcock & Browner Paul Platus, who now works with Green at advisory firm Alceon. Other shareholders are Grace Mutual chief Andrew Tyndale and property developer Alan Cardy, the second largest with 25 per cent.

HEADLINE: Fred Nile backs $20b asset deal
INTRO: The $20 billion sale of the NSW poles and wires electricity assets is guaranteed now that Fred Nile has given his commitment to back it.
TEXT:
The $20 billion sale of the NSW poles and wires electricity assets is guaranteed now that Fred Nile has given his commitment to back it.

Bankers and foreign buyers will be grateful that all the confusion and uncertainty is now resolved.

Nile told Chanticleer he will support the sale in the upper house, where he and another member of the Christian Democratic Party hold the balance of power.

Comments made by Nile before Saturday's election could have left some confused about his position in relation to the biggest government asset sale since the disposal of Telstra in three tranches over a period of 10 years.

Nile told Chanticleer he will proceed with a select committee inquiry into the poles and wires to ventilate all the issues surrounding the sale but the final report will not stand in the way of the sale going ahead.

The numbers in the NSW Legislative Council following Saturday's election means Nile no longer has to do a deal with the Shooters and Fishers Party over legislation.

In the previous Parliament, Nile and his colleague linked with the Shooters and Fishers and they voted as a block to support the Coalition government.

After Saturday's election the Coalition has 20 seats in the NSW upper house, the CDP has two, Labor has 19 and the Shooters and Fishers have two.

Nile is determined to ensure the select committee inquiry is as comprehensive as possible. He will put the proposal to the upper house when sittings resume on May 5. He says he will circulate the terms of reference to all parties before releasing them publicly.

Nile plans to call a range of witnesses including strong supporters of electricity privatisation, former federal mining minister Martin Ferguson and former NSW labor treasurer Michael Costa.

Nile said he would also call UBS Australia chief executive Matthew Grounds to question him about the circumstances surrounding changes made to a UBS report on the poles and wires which triggered a complaint from the office of the NSW Premier Mike Baird.

Goldman Sachs upsets some

Goldman Sachs can be proud of its effort at the weekend helping Chevron dispose of Caltex shares worth $4.6 billion between 4.15 pm on Friday afternoon and 2 am on Saturday morning.

It made the gutsy decision to put its balance sheet on the line before going to fund managers with the Caltex stock. That deserves a substantial financial reward.

But there can be angst and confusion if that financial reward includes incentives that some fund managers believe should have been disclosed to them.

Chanticleer knows of several unhappy fund managers who bought stock and did not know that Goldmans shared with Chevron the difference between the underwritten price of $34.20 and the final price of $35 a share.

This profit sharing arrangement gave the firm an incentive to get as high a price as possible. A straight base fee also provides an incentive to get a higher price but a share price sharing arrangement can be far more lucrative.

The fund managers interviewed by Chanticleer said if they had known about the profit sharing arrangement it would have influenced their bidding for the Caltex stock offered to them by Goldmans.

As one fund manager said: "Who are they working for? Are they working for the buyer or are they working for the seller?"

These are two of the age old questions of stock broking. However, profit sharing arrangements between vendors of stock and the principal selling the stock were not common in the good old days.

They can create perverse incentives to ramp up the sale of a share. In the Caltex case Goldmans will not say how much it shared in the upside.

But hedge funds in London have reportedly told market participants that it was a 50:50 arrangement. If that is true then Goldmans picked up $50 million on the difference between $34.20 and $35

It is not all angst out there. One fund manager said he expected Goldman to get paid properly for a "once in a generation" deal. He thought a profit sharing arrangement was not unreasonable.

However, he did say that the transaction raised the long standing question about the unequal relationship between vendors of shares and institutional buyers. All the information is in the hands of the vendor which is coming to the market with a deal that must be agreed with hours.

There was confusion on Monday as to whether block trades often involve profit sharing between the vendor and the investment bank.

Investors in Caltex, particularly those who took shares at $35 at the weekend, would be disappointed with Monday's price performance given that Goldmans told fund managers the book was covered twice.

However, one of the comforting lines going around the market is that Caltex will replace Toll Holdings in the S&P ASX 50 later this week. That will put pressure on index funds to buy the stock as well as other fund managers that track their performance against the index.

Index funds were apparently not part of the Chevron sell down at the weekend. That would fit with the story going around that market is underweight Caltex shares by about $2 billion. If that is true the stock should rise in the weeks ahead.

Boomers and the dividend rort

Dividend imputation is one of the most successful tax reforms of the past 30 years but one key element of it has become a rort that needs to be skewered in the interests of equity.

The system implemented by former Treasurer Paul Keating in 1987 never contemplated the distortions that have arisen because of the tax exemptions given to superannuation funds paying a retirement income stream as well as to super benefits earned by members aged over 60.

Dividend franking credits are flowing out of Treasury coffers each year in the form of cash payments to low tax paying entities. The equity issue arises because the beneficiaries are not necessarily low income earning people.

The cash payments by Treasury to low tax paying entities are already an important part of the $19 billion in imputation credits claimed by individuals, superannuation funds and charities.

The proportion of dividend imputation cash leaking out of the budget will grow dramatically as the baby boomers age and move into the retirement phase.

Australia is expected to lift its superannuation assets from about $1.8 trillion at December 2014 to about $6 trillion by 2030, according to the median forecast of super asset growth presented to the recent Financial System Inquiry.

If super assets are $6 trillion it is not unreasonable to assume that at least a third of that or about $2 trillion will be in the retirement phase or have beneficiaries aged over 60 and therefore pay zero tax.

The typical super fund has about 40 per cent of assets in equities paying franked dividends. If you assume dividends paid on those assets of about 4 per cent fully franked the total cash paid to these beneficiaries will be about $9 billion.

The remaining super funds in the accumulation phase, which pay tax of 15 per cent, would get estimated imputation credits of about $25 billion assuming 4 per cent fully franked dividends on average Australian equity portfolios equal to 50 per cent of assets.

Treasury has estimated the super system will grow to $9 trillion in assets by 2040.

The simple solution to the nil-tax paid rort for retirees is to exclude dividends from shareholders' taxable income. This solution was suggested by accounting firm PwC in its submission to the FSI.

It is a simple solution because it assumes the tax paid by the company does not have to be paid by the recipient. No more imputation credits would flow out of Treasury coffers.

HEADLINE: International Justice Fund pursues $40 million IPO
INTRO: The International Justice Fund may sound like a group of superheroes coming to the rescue, but they are deadly serious about an ASX-listing by June.
TEXT:
The International Justice Fund may sound like a group of superheroes coming to the rescue, but they are deadly serious about an ASX-listing by June.

Bell Potter Securities is on board to handle the float, as small-cap investors search for a viable alternative to listed litigation funder IMF.

The IJF is likely to have a market capitalisation of about $40 million and has acquired a slice of a portfolio involved in a variety of class actions, with exposure to claims worth about $160 million. It is doing roadshows, taking potential investors through the various claims and how the business works. One thing most agree on is the US model of aggressively pursuing litigation when there are big shareholder losses and murkiness over disclosure, is here to stay. The legal fraternity loves to sink its teeth into a good class action.

Street Talk can also reveal IJF has a list of acquisition opportunities, many of which it is already talking to. The team will also likely point to the performance of IMF, which listed in 1998 and is capitalised at $360 million.

IJF seed funders include Brisbane luminary Stephen Bizzell and other entities including Wavebreak Ventures. With the legal sector in the spotlight now through Slater and Gordon's British exploits, the IJF's timing appears astute.

Finally, Minter Ellison has appointed Victoria Allen to head of its Sydney mergers and acquisitions team of 16 partners and 60 lawyers. Allen has been at Minter Ellison for more than 10 years and recently advised Lloyds Group on the $1.55 billion sale of its capital finance and BOS International Australia units to Westpac Banking Corp.

The appointment comes after Minter Ellison's former head James Philips left to join DLA Piper.

HEADLINE: Investors Mutual fundie Beaumont joins Bennelong as Cuddy retires
INTRO: Bennelong Australian Equity Partners (BAEP) co-founder and chief executive Paul Cuddy is leaving the Sydney-based funds manager and will be replaced by Julian Beaumont from Investors Mutual, as revealed by Street Talk Online.
TEXT:
Bennelong Australian Equity Partners (BAEP) co-founder and chief executive Paul Cuddy is leaving the Sydney-based funds manager and will be replaced by Julian Beaumont from Investors Mutual, as revealed by Street Talk Online.

Client sources said Cuddy had announced he was planning to retire from the $5 billion Australian equities investor and was expected to leave the firm in five months' time.

Bennelong Australian Equity Partners is one of four asset management teams under the Bennelong Funds Management umbrella alongside Avoca Investment Management, Kardinia Capital and Bennelong Long Short Equity Management.

Cuddy set up BAEP in 2008 with fellow fund manager Mark East. The pair joined from ING Investment Management where they were co-heads of Australian equities.

Cuddy will be replaced by Beaumont who is expected to join BAEP as an investment director in June.

BAEP returned 17.6 per cent in the year to February, which was 3.4 per cent above the benchmark index. Its fund also gained 16.9 per cent for investors over the past five years, while the benchmark put on 7.4 per cent.

HEADLINE: Ardent Leisure investors consider getting active
INTRO: A bunch of Ardent Leisure's institutional shareholders are considering calling an extraordinary general meeting in a bid to reinstate Greg Shaw as managing director.
TEXT:
A bunch of Ardent Leisure's institutional shareholders are considering calling an extraordinary general meeting in a bid to reinstate Greg Shaw as managing director.

Almost three weeks since Shaw was replaced by former Bauer Media executive Deborah Thomas, some of the company's bigger shareholders remain disillusioned with the change despite meetings with Thomas and even chairman Neil Balnaves.

The shareholders still want to know exactly why Shaw was removed and have sought answers from the board.

The fundies accept Ardent's board wants to have a greater impact on the company's 13 million customers and increase its digital presence to help drive growth. However, they cannot understand why the board opted for a new CEO rather than beef up the marketing team.

Shaw and chief financial officer Richard Johnson were well liked by investors who trusted the pair to grow the business but also keep a close watch on Ardent's costs.

While the funds are keen to hear more from Balnaves about exactly why the change took place, they may be willing to take more drastic action should questions not be answered.

One option may be to call an extraordinary general meeting to make changes at the board level and see Shaw returned to his old job.

A shareholder needs only a 5 per cent stake to call the meeting. More problematic is ensuring more than half of voting shareholders would approve the motion in order to be successful at the shareholder meeting.

Activists would need support of 30 to 40 per cent of the shareholder register, assuming 60 to 80 per cent of shares are voted at the meeting.

It's a tough task but has been done before, including at Redflex Holdings in 2009.

HEADLINE: Providence shapes as strong contender for Crown assets
INTRO: Private equity giant Providence Equity Partners is through to the business end of Crown Castle Australia's auction, sources close to the $1.5 billion-plus telecommunication tower business told Street Talk on Monday.
TEXT:
Private equity giant Providence Equity Partners is through to the business end of Crown Castle Australia's auction, sources close to the $1.5 billion-plus telecommunication tower business told Street Talk on Monday.

Providence, which has $US40 billion under management, is expected to join a handful of bidders who will attend management presentations over the coming weeks.

The bidding line-up includes a handful of infrastructure investors, including Macquarie Group's Macquarie Infrastructure and Real Assets, Canada's Brookfield Infrastructure, and New Zealand's Morrison & Co.

Providence's interest in the local telco infrastructure business comes after a similar investment in Brazil.

The private equity firm owns Brazilian mobile-phone tower operator Grupo TorreSur, which leases tower space to telecommunications providers. TorreSur is the fastest growing operator of its type in Latin America, as well as the largest independent wireless tower company in Brazil, according to its website. It owns and operates more than 6000 towers.

Providence also invested $430 million in Aditya Birla Telecom in 2008, which holds a stake in Indus Towers - a company formed to combine the wireless assets of three of India's largest GSM mobile operators.

It has also kicked tyres on other Australian targets in recent months, including Ten Network Holdings and Hoyts Group.

Final bids for Crown Castle are expected in the first half of May, although bidders are waiting on a specific date.

Greenhill Australia is advising Providence.

As Street Talk first reported in January, minority shareholders had Credit Suisse running a sale for a 22.4 per cent stake in Crown Castle. However, the indicative round turned in some big numbers, with a few of the buyers making offers for the entire business. Crown Castle International added its stake to the auction and Morgan Stanley was hired to run the sale alongside its Swiss rival.

Potential buyers are expected to value Crown Castle at about $1.5 billion or 18-times earnings.

Elsewhere, PanAust bidder Guangdong Rising was believed to be in the market for the copper and gold company's shares on Monday. It's understood GRAM picked up more than 10 million shares worth just over 1 per cent of the shareholder register. It would take the company's stake above 23.5 per cent. A substantial shareholder notice is expected in coming days.

Finally, Gilbert + Tobin is advising the majority of Atlas Iron's US term lenders alongside Houlihan Lokey on a potential restructuring deal. Lazard Australia is advising the company.
